rv.q: It’s an arresting but oddly distancing experience, as if you’re watching two plays at once, your brain constantly trying to unpick them.
In real estate terms: ambitious, masses of potential — but not quite the finished article.
It's a fascinating idea, and while it would be odd to see this without at least having seen the film for reference, I'd say it's an experiment that works.
While there’s something wearying about seeing yet another West End stage filled with men, their issues and their egos, this is a potent and dismayingly timely revival.
But, collectively, this reinvention has the aura of a rehearsal room exercise in which accomplished actors sketch personalities without, for the most part, getting to the heart of the characters.

This minimalism might be efficient, but it doesn't always serve the play, and makes it harder to create the claustrophobic, cigarette smoke-saturated feel of a tiny office that's full of caged corporate beasts.
Instead they’re offering something slick but decaffeinated, evasive and artificial.
The experience is impressive, but it hasn’t got that snarling bite-your-leg quality that makes it such a repulsive and compelling work.
For all its promise, the purpose of the gender reversal here feels unresolved.
If we accept this purely as a means to allow fantastic actresses to sink their teeth into these roles... then it’s a cheer-worthy enterprise.
The cast is exceptional and does a fantastic job of hooking the audience into the murky world of real estate.
Yet for all its conceptual tricks, the production lacks an electricity that should have been supercharged in Rob Howell’s claustrophobia-inducing in the round staging.
This new production, directed by Patrick Marber, has an all-female cast and a shifted perspective that is bold and thought-provoking, if not always theatrically successful.
The evening is admirable in its reach if sometimes confounding in its result, but the abilility of Glengarry to sear the soul here proves as elusive as this play's most-wanted leads.
In the main however, I found too many jarring incongruities to make it plausible.
If I went with low expectations, Patrick Marber’s production turns out to be both unsettling and fascinating.
What really drove the story was the strong performances of Marber’s all-female cast.
With huge scope for a more in-depth analysis of female dynamics in a cutthroat corporate environment, Glengarry Glen Ross feels like a missed opportunity for this stellar cast.
Even so, it feels like a synthetic, vaguely modish experiment.
Exaggerated characters and poor pacing lead to a rare misstep for the Old Vic, made all the more disappointing given what a knockout this production ought to have been if it hadn’t fallen through.
This revival may not unlock many new dimensions within Mamet‘s play but it is compelling enough to remind us why it continues to be an intriguing and engrossing drama.
The plot of Glengarry Glen Ross retains its surprises and is particularly effective if you have not seen the play or film previously.
This is a bold revival of a modern classic, even if it never quite capitalises on the opportunities presented by its central concept.
Glengarry Glen Ross has incredible performances from almost all of the cast but it remains a cynical, nasty reminder of the yuppie heights of greed in the 1980s under Reagan and Thatcher.

cn.t: This all-female revival of Mamet's toxic masculinity classic divides critics. Strong performances are widely praised, but many question whether the gender-swap concept fully delivers on its intriguing premise.
